To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the reactivity and spectroscopic properties of the nitrosyl adducts of ferrous hemes and of the negatively charged σ-adduct of 1,3.5-trinitro-benzene are strongly dependent on the nature of the metal center and on the nature of anion, respectively.

the reactivity of NO with ferric and with ferrous hemes is remarkably similar in the gas phase; and that the σ-addition of anions to π-deficient arenes leads to the formation of weakly covalently bound σ-complexes.
(i) NO adducts of hemes are highly labile in vacuo, and that (ii) the anion binding motifs to the 1,3-5-trinitro-benzene molecule are highly dependent on the nature of the anion.

the study of the structure and reactivity of metal–ligand and anion–π complexes by IRMPD experiments in combination with quantum chemical calculations.
the investigation of molecular complexes, both biological and synthetic, in the gas phase and in the condensed phase.
a variety of systems, ranging from biological to organic intermediates, and with the development of new spectroscopic tools to investigate them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IRMPD technique is a valuable tool to probe the coordination chemistry of metal–ligand complexes and the binding modes of organic anions.

the IRMPD spectroscopic approach is a valuable tool for investigating the nature of the interaction between the anion and the arene in σ-complexes and for the determination of the structure of anionic intermediates, which are of fundamental importance in organic and biological processes.
, in the absence of a strong metal–ligand covalency, the IRMPD spectra of σ-complexes are not diagnostic of the anion binding mode.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the IRMPD spectra of anion–arenes have revealed that anions can be considered to be π-electron donors, as the anion–areno complexes display the same structural motifs as those of π-electron donor ligands.
the gas phase is a valuable tool for the study of biological and organic intermediates, providing a reliable reference for the interpretation of spectroscopic data in solution.

the IRMPD spectroscopic method, in conjunction with DFT calculations, is a powerful tool for the characterization of the molecular structures and the determination of the binding motifs for both neutral and ionic intermediates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the anion–arenes are not just a chemical curiosity but they can be used as a model system for the study of anion–arenetriyl radicals, which are important intermediates in organic chemistry.

the gas phase can be a valuable tool for the study of the electronic and vibrational properties of the complexes under investigation, providing information that is often difficult or impossible to obtain by other techniques.

the spectroscopic signatures of the NO and anion–aren complexes are highly sensitive to the nature and coordination of the metal center, the electronic properties of the π-electron-deficit arene, and the basicity of the anions.
